utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Thursday, 14th of May, 2009. Good morning, Mr. Praljak. Good morning, Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Pusic, and Mr. Stojic. And good morning to the Defence counsel and the entire OTP bench, with Mr. Stringer and his associates. Good morning to all the people assisting us. General Praljak's testimony is going to continue today. Without further adieu, I'll ask Ms. Pinter to proceed, and wishing her a good morning, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. It's not Mr. Kovacic, but we'll try and be efficient. With your permission, Your Honour, I'd like to give the original book of -- entitled "Assistance to the Republic of Croatia," which is 3D02633 first, because the e-court print is a very poor quality so it's difficult to read the text in Croatian. The book has been translated from cover to cover, and it is to be found in the binder called "Aid of the Republic of Croatia to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: So it's not "Assistants to," interpreter's correction, but "Aid of."

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And with your permission, I'd like to hand the book over, through the usher, to General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, 3D02633 is the document number. It is a book called "Aid of the Republic of Croatia to the Muslim and Bosniak People in the BH Army," in the course of 1991 until 1995. It says that the author is Slobodan Praljak. What can you tell the Court about how this book came into being, and its contents, in general terms?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This book is a collection of documents setting out the facts about all the political and military leadership's actions during the aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina, how they assisted -- how the Croatian leadership assisted Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, how it assisted the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Muslim and Bosniak people. In preparing for this trial, we collected documents together, and they were gathered and take up 92 binders, as you know. They were brought to The Hague, and I think that the CD-ROMs were handed over to the OTP and the Tribunal. And of this vast amount of material, which as I say takes up as many as 92 binders, we selected just the most characteristic documents. So these are the facts which will help us to arrive at the truth in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And can you tell us what the sources of these documents were?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The source was the archives, the Croatian State Archive, the archive of the Croatian Army, and some of the documents I received from -- or we received from, rather, some Muslims who took part in these activities on the territory of the Republic of Croatia; that is to say, those who were in the centres for training, unit training centres, or logistic support centres for the Main Staff of the BH Army, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Was there any cooperation with the Office for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I think that we can take this document by document. I seem to be having a problem with the microphone, so I have to adjust my position. But I'd like to start off with page 3D -- I'm going to read out the pages of the book for the Croatian and English versions so that we can all follow. 3D32-1023 is the first one. That's right, that's the page. And this is when the humanitarian crisis reached its peak in December 1992. We discussed that yesterday, and I thought you could tell us something about this map. Now, on e-court, please. May it be placed on e-court for the others? It's much easier to see and read.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is the information that other people have testified about here, too, but it says that at the peak of the humanitarian crisis in December 1992, there were 402.768 refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina in Croatia and 260.000 displaced persons, and the number never dropped below 195.000 refugees and 183.000 displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Judge Trechsel has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think it is - I'm speaking for the Bench - we are not quite aware of what we should be looking at or could be looking at. What we have on e-court is, on the left side, a map. Now I see, on the right side, we have something else, and perhaps we can also be told what page number it is. But the map we do not have in our file, and it is also in Croatian, and we have no translation either. So it is probably not, itself, very useful. And I think what we now have is page 6. And having found out, I apologise for the interruption. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's precisely what I wanted to say. Each map has been translated, but it's not on the map, it's on a piece of paper and text beside the map. But I will give the English page numbers in future, so I hope there won't be any problem in finding your way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, General, as you have the original book, without the e-court page numbers, I suggest that you leaf through the book, and I'll give the page numbers.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am referring to how many from the area -- well, we're dealing with the end of 1992. And the Serbs -- I'm saying what territory the Serbs took control of and how many people they expelled. 15.000 to 20.000 Muslims were expelled from Republika Srpska and came to Zenica. The same amount came to Travnik, Muslims, that is, 15.000 to 20.000. There were about 20.000 expelled Muslims in Bugojno, for example. With the fall of Jajce, about 15.000 Croats were displaced and expelled and about 12.000 Muslims, and so on and so forth. And they scattered, most people that went to Croatia. But most of the population remained in the Lasva Valley, Uskoplje, Bugojno, or rather Gornji Vakuf and that General area, which of course changed the ethnic structure, and the consequences of that is something that I have already spoken at length about. And I think that Ms. Thatcher had a lot to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, General, would you take a look at the chapter entitled "Croatian Assistance to the BH Army," and it is 2092, the document, and in English it's 3D38 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly slow down when quoting numbers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Pinter, the interpreters are telling us that they do not have the text, so that when you read quickly, it's a really huge problem for them. Do endeavour to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The interpreters have texts of all these documents. I have to say that. Our case manager has handed them over. But I will slow down. So in English, the page is 3D38-0010. The Croatian page is 3D32-1025.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, now "Help in Armament to the BH Army" is this chapter. And would you tell the Court what the most important documents there are that you'd like to point out and focus on and which say how much Croatia helped in arming the BH Army? But I'd like to remind you that we've heard quite a lot about that in the proceedings so far.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, the total -- well, the quantified data, we have 801 documents, with 3.820 military articles continuously sent to the BH Army, or items, and we have a smaller number of issue documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just a moment, General. The general is referring to 3D38-0012, or in English -- that's the English. In Croatian, it is 3D32-1027.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The greatest assistance went by air towards Bihac Airport, Coralici and the 5th Corps of the BH Army. That was an air drop. And while possible, they flew to Sarajevo, but then afterwards different avenues were pursued. The planes that were successfully used to obtain weapons would land at airports in Zagreb, Pula, and Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The next page is 3D38-0013 of the English and 3D32-1028 of the Croatian. And what does that relate to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It relates to the transport of military equipment and weapons from Pula to Coralic by plan, from Zagreb to Coralic, and they flew towards Zenica for as long as they could, and then from Zenica it was taken to Gorazde. And that was driven by the BH Army towards Srebrenica and Gorazde, because BH Army helicopters were procured via Croatia, the pilots were trained there, and there were some unfortunate incidents. So a helicopter crashed once at Pleso Airport because it was overloaded and couldn't take the heavy load of weapons, and there was a big explosion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The next map relates to a transport by land, and it is 3D38-0014 or 3D32-1029 in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A little slower, please, with the numbers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the main route taking weapons to the BH Army, Split, and then in different ways crossing -- by Imotski, there was a crossing point towards Tomislavgrad, which is not on the map, and then it went by via Rumboci, Rama, Gornji Vakuf, Bugojno, towards -- well, there were two ways. One went directly to the Main Logistics Centre of the BH Army in Visoko, and a lot went directly to the 3rd Corps, to the various brigades, and so on and so forth. And a large number of people were involved in all this, and everybody fended for themselves, did what they could with respect to the convoys, except for the main portion that went directly to the Logistics Base at Visoko. And Mr. Rasim Delic, who was later the chief of the Main Staff of the BH Army, compiled a report as to what they had received, and we have that. And three or four times as much went directly to Sarajevo, Gorazde, or Mostar through various channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, please. Excuse me, please. I must confess that I'm a bit lost -- not lost in translation, lost in detail this time. I absolutely accept, although it is not contested, and we've heard plenty of evidence about it, that you want to show some more about how Croatia assisted the Muslims, to put it in one word. I do not understand why you go into details such as the roads taken or what was transported by helicopter and what was transported by plane. I simply cannot see in what respect this is relevant, but perhaps you can explain why you think that these details, even, are connected to the indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the indictment, Judge Trechsel, there are two points. First of all, the main charge is that the political and military leadership of Croatia wanted to cut off a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina and an exit to Croatia, the so-called Banovina. And then it is necessary to stipulate that the air force planes, helicopters, and so on did quite the opposite of what one would expect if that were the case. If you wanted to take something away from a country and state, you don't supply their army in this way. And, secondly, I indicated this route passing through Herceg-Bosna. So if the Prosecutor claims that Herceg-Bosna wanted to separate and that it was -- and that there was parallel statehood and it wanted to secede and expel the Muslims and destroy the state, then how come Herceg-Bosna allowed all these convoys to go through throughout that time and to reach the BH Army? And once that army, the BH Army in individual areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina had those weapons, they turned it towards the HVO. I think that's very clear. So I it's clear why we need to look at all this to see what the quantities were, how this was done, and what period it covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, for the record, I must say it is, to me, the details are not clear. If it is established, it's not even contested that huge amounts of material went to the ABiH and to the Muslims in general. Then it doesn't add anything to say that it was also transported over their territory because, I mean, there's no other way. But, I mean, I think it's hopeless to try to concentrate this to the essential. And, I don't know, if my colleagues don't intervene, I will leave it at that. But I must really say that I'm not convinced at all that this enormous detail is necessary, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me, I will answer. We don't have any facts that have been established. We have the indictment, which is as broad as it is. We have the indictment with the scope which is huge. And we cannot afford not to call every little shred of evidence to show what was done in those years, what the Republic of Croatia did to show that there was no plan and that there was no idea about the joint criminal enterprise that would include leadership of the Republic of Croatia and the accused present in this courtroom; that this claim cannot stand. But we did not receive from the Prosecution or, indeed, from the Trial Chamber any decision to the effect, You don't have to call any evidence, because we know that this is a fact. Then we wouldn't be calling any evidence on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just wanted to say, based on what I heard from you, Judge Trechsel, it would appear that we -- that the Bench is taking judicial notice that, in fact, the weapons did come; they came from Croatia, and that -- and that's why the detail is not necessary. So if we have -- if the Bench is united on that, that this is a fact that is established, then perhaps we don't need to go into the details. You know, so this would be considered an established fact, you know. So if the Bench is taking judicial notice, then I believe -- you know, I would concur with you in that aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I think this might be a very useful road to save time, but, of course, we want to hear what the Prosecution has to say to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And good morning, Mr. President, and Your Honours. I don't think there's really any dispute that arms supplies moved into Bosnia and Herzegovina through Croatia. I think the dispute is about where those supplies went ultimately, whether they went to supply ABiH units, for example, fighting in the Tuzla region, who fought together with the HVO throughout the conflict, the Bihac region in the north-western part of the country of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I think there's -- the divergence is the places where those arms were going, as well as the time-frames involved, and the extent to which the arms supplies dried up in the Herzegovina region or in those areas where the HVO was in direct military conflict with the ABiH. And so I think we all agree that arms went in. I think the dispute relates to where they were going and the time-frames involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I thank the gentleman for that admission. However, it must be borne in mind that you have routes that go through various territories, you have a very fluid situation throughout this period, things are changing. And of course weapons may be intended for one particular area, they may -- some may arrive there, some may turn back, and to suggest that somehow they were going to one particular destination, they all went there and remained there and they were used for the very purposes for which they were given, is another thing. I think what the general wishes to do, the way I understand it, is to show the complexity in the locations of where these routes were, because then it becomes very important to show that the Croats knew at some point that those weapons in all likelihood could very well be used against them, but nonetheless, because they were committed to a Bosnia and Herzegovina, they went along and provided those weapons. And I think that those details are what the general is trying to demonstrate, the routes and what have you, because in some places they could have easily choked the route, in which case the weapons would not have gone through. And, again, while the Prosecution -- I understand what they're saying. They want to compartmentalise this as if Croats in the Posavina somehow think differently than the Croats in Central Bosnia, or, you know, they're willing to cooperate in one area, but fight in another. We're saying it's a very fluid situation, the situation changes from place to place, but nonetheless the Croatian government at this time, with the assistance and insistence of the big powers, in particular the United States, is allowing massive amounts of weapons to be coming in from places like Iran and Saudi Arabia and what have you. So that's why the general is trying to go through the detail. But if we can all agree on all of this, then I'm certainly willing to go along in saving time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I wonder whether it is possible to stream-line the evidence in the -- or to the areas which are really disputed; namely, I quote you, Mr. Karnavas, on what went -- was destined, for instance, for Posavina and then when was detoured. And it seems to me that to a large extent what is essential is perhaps more the intention of the Croatian government than what actually happened, although you correctly pointed out that at some times they must have had some sort of dolus eventualis, that part of it would finally explode in their own face. If it were possible to stream-line the evidence so that we are close to problem areas, then that would be useful, very useful for the Chamber. The problem is that with the details we've heard now, we are in the void. It's almost single grains of sand that should perhaps one day give a mosaic picture, but it is not possible to place them at the moment. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I could just make one suggestion -- I think -- that relates to what's being said. I'm going to avoid the invitation to make a closing speech on this, because I think -- I mean, you know, we can all argue about what it means, but that's for a later day. Now, we have maps here, we have indications of material going to various locations. What we don't have on any of this, for example, is the time-frame, and the general hasn't spoken about that. And that's, in the Prosecution point of view, an important issue. Maybe Ms. Pinter is going to go there, and we're just anticipating the next line of questions. But again it's, in our view, not very helpful at all if we have these generalities without even any time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Madam Nozica, but I would only like to say the following: that, of course, we are ready to listen to the witness and to the Defence, Mr. Praljak, and at the same time I also feel that, for example, we have this very huge volume here only in B/C/S. Now, frankly, I mean -- most of it in B/C/S, and somehow we are getting lost in that abundance of material. So my point is also that probably the Defence in the matter could help us to find really the most important elements of the material in the documents and not to be lost everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: All in English. This is all in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Okay. So I thank Judge Trechsel. So then, but in other words, I'm not really speaking about the translation; I am speaking about the material which has been presented to us and which means that at the same time during the last couple of months, we have received a great number of other documents through other witnesses, and like also the Stojic witness, et cetera -- witnesses. And that is why I believe that it would be really a better way to choose if the Praljak Defence would find the opportunity to help us to concentrate on the major issues here and not to get lost in the details. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I didn't take the floor - it doesn't happen often - but I wanted to give the opportunity for everyone to speak up in order to understand what everyone's position was. First and foremost, the Trial Chamber did not deliberate on this issue of the judicial notice that might be made regarding weapons supply, so each Judge takes the floor on his own behalf. And up until now, I insist to say that so far the Trial Chamber has not deliberated on the facts and on the liabilities that might be incurred by each and every one. This is absolutely clear, which means that all the evidence submitted by the Defence, as well as by the Prosecution, is evidence that will be assessed according to two criteria: relevance and probative value. And the final assessment can only be done at the very end of this trial. So as of now, I must say that, personally, I'm still in a complete fog, in the dark, you know. And I'm moving cautiously, step by step, to try to understand what happened, what the Prosecutor is alleging in the indictment, and what Defence is actually saying also. We've just had a debate here in this courtroom. Mr. Stringer highlighted a couple of points in this -- a couple of points that are very important to understand things. First, he said that we absolutely needed dates to know when the weapons were supplied. We need the time-frame. Did these deliveries go on throughout 1992 and 1993, up until the first months of 1994? This is crucial to see if there was a continuous supply of arms, of weapons. Then the second very important point for everyone, we need to know whether these weapons were for the entire ABiH, and the last document we just saw, where obviously the arms are to be supplied to Visoko, we need to know whether after Visoko, all these weapons would be redistributed throughout all ABiH units or, as the Prosecutor seems to allege, whether these weapons were only to be provided to a number of units in a number of places. These two items are essential, and here I fully agree with the Prosecution; we absolutely need to have a good time reference for all this, and we need to know exactly how these weapons were dispatched. If we have a clear understanding of this, I believe that we will be able to move forward. Now, on the other hand, and here I share the point of view of my fellow Judges, is it that important to really look at all the documents regarding 1992? We've already seen a wealth of documents regarding this year. That's a big problem. Maybe Mr. Praljak would better focus on 1993. As you know, 1993 is a year where we have very important dates; January 5, for example, May 9, April 30th, the entire month of June. There are some key moments in 1993, and then we have everything that happened after June. But let me tell you, Mr. Praljak, this whole drawing you made with the trucks and the trucks routes, it's very interesting because we see it originates from Zagreb or Rijeka, goes to Split, ends up in Visoko, and we see that it has to go through Gornji Vakuf and Travnik territories, which is fine. But did this happen in 1992? Did this happen in 1993? Did this happen during the conflict, in the midst of it? We absolutely have to have some information on this. So give us maybe less details, but give us relevant details that have probative value. While I was listening to everyone, I was looking at the binder, the one in B/C/S, not the one in English but the one in B/C/S. And I saw that in this binder we have a number of documents regarding August 1993. That might be very important. I think everybody gave their opinion, and now it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understand that you know the relevance, that it is up to you to decide on the relevance. But the indictment that I've read, the joint criminal enterprise begins in 1991. The joint criminal enterprise in the heads begins in 1991, according to the charges against us. If it begins in 1991, then these documents show that it doesn't, it doesn't begin in 1991, and it goes on into 1992. Well, we're not stupid, so these documents tell us, no, in 1992 there was no such thing. Furthermore, of course, if I were a judge deciding on this, I would say, Okay, it's enough to show just a couple of documents to prove that this did not exist. But on our part, there is something that is called fear, fear of the indictment, of the charges. I have my own opinion of it, but this fear of this indictment has made me go into too many details, to be too broad. Of course, I cannot decide what is relevant. It is up to you to do it. Well, I am afraid, not physically, but I'm afraid of the prevailing logic here. So I'm saying this: Throughout the war, arms were going to the BH Army in Visoko, Your Honours. Visoko is the central logistics base of the BH Army. And if the commander, chief of their Main Staff, Sefer Halilovic, or Rasim Delic, decides to launch this Offensive 93, and if I or we give them weapons to Visoko, who decides who will get those weapons, which unit? They own the weapons. They can distribute them as they see fit. And, of course, they send it to Jablanica, to Mostar, because what will the BH Army use by way of weapons, what will it use to fire upon the enemy in this Offensive 93 if it doesn't have any weapons? And the only source of weapons for them is Croatia. And this should be it, in terms of solving this problem logically. But this logic is familiar to me. I know every detail of it, but I don't know whether you can understand it, and that's why I went into such detail. Of course, we will narrow it down, not only as regards the weapons, but the overall aid. I will tell you what was going on, on the plan of sports, humanitarian organisations, sports. Croatia was the only way in which Bosnia and Herzegovina could survive, Croats and Muslims alike. Now let me say one more thing. Apart from the weapons in Visoko -- and you will see a report from Rasim Delic about the quantity of weapons that came into Croatia in 1993. And three or four times as many weapons came in through other channels to individual units of BH Army. For instance, we were sending some weapons to Sarajevo, and people smuggled weapons in. And it is also the truth, when the BH Army attacked the HVO, when the conflict broke out, we in Croatia, and I will show you documents where it says, Let Praljak decide about some training - I have it here - we started smuggling things around Zagreb, in some parts controlled by the Croatian Army around Zagreb. There were small devices where we put weapons into food. We took out food from the containers and put in weapons, because I said already there was this huge problem. I was fighting people who were attacking me, and at the same time I knew -- I was aware of and I was approving the transfer of weapons to the same army, and that was going on throughout the war. As I said, after the conflict started, there were some problems, but we were lying to ourselves; we were lying to our own fighters, Your Honours. This is what I'm claiming. This is my evidence. I have proof of that. I have a person who testified about that, a Muslim who was working on it, and he will come here, and he will testify as to how weapons were smuggled to BH Army. And, Ms. Nika, could you please look at the establishment of logistic centres of the BH Army in Croatia and get me the dates?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but let me just respond to the Trial Chamber that we started with the maps in order to give you an overview, and it is not our intention to go through all those documents. But, on the other hand, in order to be able to tender this book into evidence, we have to deal with some documents and all the chapters in order to be able to ask for it to be tendered into evidence, because it is a compendium of documents put together in one place. And only when you get all the documents in one place can you get the whole picture. You cannot get the whole picture from disjointed pieces, to see the forms and shapes that this aid took. And the Defence is trying to give you as many facts as possible in order for your decision to be based on those facts and in order for you to be -- to have all the data at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Let us now look at -- well, I don't really have it. We should look at yours.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Training centres, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, look at the chapter on the training of BH pilots in Croatia. I have a chapter here on unit establishment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question for you, Mr. Praljak. You mentioned Halilovic, saying that Croatia, through the HVO, supplied -- or that the HVO supplied weapons to the ABiH. Very well. Unfortunately, here you know that each party has to submit its own evidence. In a civil law system, we would have asked Mr. Halilovic whether he actually received weapons and how he actually distributed the weapons, and that would have saved everyone a lot of time. Now, General Praljak, I'd like to know whether you envisaged to actually call any of your adversaries as witnesses in your case, you know, high-level adversaries, so that they could confirm what you're actually saying, or do you believe that this is impossible to have these people come and testify for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, an associate did try to talk to two people, but they refused, so that was impossible. But there is a report. We have that. It's a regular report by Rasim Delic about what was procured from Croatia just for the base in Visoko, and we're going to show you that, show you the document. It's a very extensive document. So it's his document, not mine. These aren't my documents. They're documents mostly related to units organised by the Muslims, transported by Muslims, where the truck-drivers were Muslims, so those are the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this book, there are documents which relate to a number of topics, and they are enumerated in the contents list. Now, all the questions that Judge Antonetti raised with respect to the period of time, the year, the critical dates as far as the indictment is concerned and so on, we have documents on that. However, I think we're going to lose our way if we keep skipping things. We're going to skip 1992, but I think that, General, we should take this in the order it is set out to look at the documents that are essential in order to show what the situation was like with respect to Croatian aid to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and thereby we would be refuting the charges and allegations in the indictment which say that the politics in Croatia and the HZ-HB had the intention to undertake a joint criminal enterprise and the intention to cut off part of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So I'd like to ask you, General, that we go through the topics. We're going to skip the years, skip 1992 and skip some documents, but go through the material in general. So you don't have the page numbers; I do. I will give the page numbers, and you can just tell us what the documents are. Otherwise, we'll never get through it. We'll get through --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's do March, when there was a conflict in Rama.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Are we dealing with 1993 and Gojko Susak? The document on the right, I believe, shows you that. I'll give the page number. Now, the 1st of March, 1993, the Ministry Of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. The letter is from Ante Jelavic, and it is a list of the resources confiscated from the BH Army which were being sent to the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. It's 3D32-1035 or, rather -- well, the number's the same, it's the same number. I don't seem to have the number of the English page, but it is 3D38-0016, I think. And then we can go on to the next document, and the date after that is the 6th of March.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, the 6th of March, where there are already conflicts in Uskoplje and Rama and Novi Travnik, and I knew -- well, Your Honours, if you read the document dated the 13th of January where I talked to the high-ranking French delegation, I expressly say that the war will continue and what the political options are -- of the individual sides are. And from that, you can see that we were fully conscious of the fact that the conflict would probably break out, and you'll see how much effort we put in to prevent the conflict breaking out. But, anyway, here on the 6th of March, a vast quantity of weapons were being sent, and you've already mentioned this 6th of March document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D38-0024 is the number?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down and speak one at a time and state the -- read the numbers slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're lost with the numbers over here. We're just moving too fast, and we're not able to keep up. We're trying to take notes of which documents we might object to or not object to, and it's impossible the way we're going here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Pinter, give the number of the document in B/C/S so that Mr. Praljak can look at the document, and at the same time give the number in English, of the English page, so that each and every one can see and follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, take the binder up, because you have the Croatian page numbers there, and look at the original as well. That's the only way we can proceed. Otherwise, the Prosecution won't be able to follow, and that won't be a good thing. Now, we reached 3D32-1040. That was the page number, to simplify matters. My learned friend Mr. Kovacic wants me to tell you that we're referring to the same document all the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter can't catch the number. Too fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... It is "Aid by the Republic of Croatia to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." So I don't give the main numbers all the time, because I said at the very beginning that it was one document, and that is 3D02633, and there are a series of documents there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've found it. It is the 5th of March, 1993, and you can give the English number.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D38-0025 is the English reference. That's right. Now we can move on. You leaf through the document --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next date is the 6th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, please. This document, 0025, is dated 5 March. It is from the Croatian Army Main Staff, and some material is to be issued for Grude Logistics Base. I was of the opinion that Grude was the headquarters of Mate Boban and a place of the HVO, but I thought that the purpose was to show that material went to the ABiH. And can I -- do I misunderstand something, overlook something which indicates that this, in fact, was material for the ABiH and not for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the problem is that you've already heard witnesses who have -- they were Bosniaks, Muslims, who took over weapons in Grude, at the logistics base there of the HVO at Grude. Now, by this we wish to demonstrate and are demonstrating that the logistics base in Grude received weapons, that weapons were coming in, and the source of those weapons, if you look at the documents, we'll see -- or, rather, you'll see where those weapons were sent on to further. So these documents show where the trucks could have left from or -- well, the general wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, we have heard testimony from witnesses here who said how many weapons from Grude went to the BH Army. A portion went to Grude first and was then sent on to the BH Army, and another part went directly to Visoko, as I said. The third part went to other places. And if we look at the document of the 6th of March, 1993, the next document, we'll be able to see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, just a moment, please. Could the Court and the Trial Chamber look at 3D38-0024 now, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what's the Croatian number?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The Croatian number is 38 -- 3D32-1039. The date is the same. It's the 6th of March, 1993, and this is instructions for the issuance of equipment for the requirements of Grude, and MTS taken over by Mr. Sujab from Sarajevo, and the equipment will be transported in the following vehicles. And the trucks are listed, with their drivers. General, the drivers of these trucks --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it goes to Zenica, and they were all Muslims. They were all trucks from Zenica, going to Zenica, and we only wrote down that it was going to Grude, whereas it was being dispatched directly to Zenica. And the drivers were Muslim drivers, driving for the BH Army. So I think some things are so clear, and we've been repeating them umpteen times that there can be no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, General, the 6th of March, 1993, 3D32 is the Croatian, 3D32-1042. The English is 3D38-0027. And that is a letter sent to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, that's who it's addressed to, and it is sent by the BH Army and the Logistics Centre in Zagreb. The coordinator is Azim Karamehmedovic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I've been trying to say throughout. The BH Army, on the 6th of March, after a series of conflicts had already taken place, there were things going on in Konjic already, and everything was clear to us already. Well, we weren't stupid down there not to realise what was going on, neither in Croatia or in Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the 6th of March, and we'll see this later on, too, there was a logistics centre in Zagreb, of the army of another state which is taking over what is listed in this document and is driving it to Zenica, transporting it to Zenica, and they're all Muslims. This man, Stipo Blazevic, he's a Croat. But all the others are Muslims. And the coordinator of all this is Engineer Azim Karamehmedovic who was in the logistics centre of the BH Army in Zagreb. And the criminal enterprise has been going on, according to the Prosecution, for already two years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, a question [indiscernible]. This document of March 6th on the delivery of weapons to Zenica, could you tell us whether at the time, in March, you knew that the 7th Brigade was stationed in Zenica? The 7th Brigade was the strong -- it was part of the 3rd Corps; did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I knew about the 7th, the 17th, the Mujahedin. I was well informed. I was totally informed about everything. As you will hear later on, we still hoped that he -- we would be able to prevent the conflict. I'm going to show it very clearly on my own example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may further to clarify. It appears to me, and I stand, of course, to be corrected, that the documents from, in English, 0024 to 0027, are all very closely linked together. They always seem to come up, those 100.000 bullets and the thousand 152-millimetre rounds. One document shows - that's 25 - that they are to be delivered to Grude. Then there is an order that they -- that was 26, I think. And then there's the letter of 6th March which says who is going to pick it up. We have again the same number. And then we have the drivers that pick them up at 24. Is that correct? Are all these four documents concerning, inter alia, the exactly same parcel of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see that from the names of the drivers, the registration plates. And we started with Grude to show the origins of the loads, but they are connected by the dates, by the sequence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, therefore, here, then, some things do go to Gradacac, but they are destined for the 1st and 2nd Corps, for the units of the 106th as well. However, the main escort of the convoy, Mr. Emir Beslagic, hails from Visoko. And all this has been taken to Visoko. Please we're not -- I know, I understand all the questions. But look here, if you're delivering a thousand shells for 152-millimetre calibre weapons, then this is not exactly a small quantity. It's not peanuts, is it? You can go on, Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that we can move on to the next topic, Mr. Stojic's Defence has already presented so much evidence and so many documents about the arms.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could, please, the shuffling in the courtroom stop, because we can't follow anything in the booths.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at the document 3D32-1051. This is the 7th April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. I would like to provide the Trial Chamber with the English number, which I don't have because I did not prepare it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: English?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This is Croatian. I don't have the English.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's the 7th April. It's already April 1993, and it says the Main Staff of the HVO has approved an unhindered passage of the MTS. A list is then given of all the vehicles, with their loads, how many bullets; 1 million; RPG rockets, 1.048 pieces; automatic rifle, 305 pieces; Maljutka, seven pieces. That's for anti-armour defence. This was on the 7th of April, 1993. And then I don't know whether you have it on your list, 18 February 1993, two transport helicopters were purchased, MI8T [phoen] for the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This is 3D32-1052, but I still don't have the English pages.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, never mind. It's neither here nor there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I can assist, it might be 3D38-0035.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This refers to the document dated 18 February, 1993, or the previous one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The 7th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nika, let's move on, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Please go to 3D32-1061. In English, this is 3D38-0047.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This is a report, i.e., a letter to the Office for National Security of Croatian Report Service. The date is 10 May, 1999. The Ministry of the Interior Service for Protection Constitutional Order of the Republic of Croatia. General, what do you know about the allegations in this document and about this document, in general?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also know that all the staff from the BH Army who were working in Croatia were allowed to obtain communications tools. We have evidence to that, and we will see about (redacted), because I personally approved for lost quantities of communication equipment to be given to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And here it is stated very clearly in the third paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Praljak. We might need to redact, because you mentioned a witness for whom you sought protective measures.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all the microphones which are not in use please be switched off. Thank you. Could the counsel please turn on the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Luckily enough, the name on the record is not correct, but I would still like to thank you, Your Honour, for making sure that the person is protected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the third paragraph, there is a reference to all the persons who came to collect all that and the places where all that went to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Registrar, can you please prepare a redacting order; page 27, line 23. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, can you now go to the packing of food products. 3D32-1084 is the page number. We are talking about UNHCR trucks, weapons packaged in food stuff packaging. The English page is 3D38-0078, Croatian page 3D32-1084.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a cluster of documents testifying to the fact that -- or, rather, how all that was done. This is especially important in the case of Bihac, because in addition to the helicopter and the aircraft flights, of which some were brought down and they could not have transported enough for such a huge corps. Among the personnel of the United Nations and UNHCR there was people who, when they returned from Bihac, having seen what the situation was like over there, and who was attacking whom over there, and what could happen there, and how people fared over there, they simply, for their humanitarian reasons and motives, that's the only interpretation I have, they violated the rules of their own service. That's how I interpret the whole thing. I don't think this was permissible. However, when some provisions of the law are contrary to the moral feelings of an individual, certain individuals opt for their moral sentiments rather than for the letter of the law. And they -- these people then agreed to transport weapons in the food packaging, and this was all done with the knowledge of Franjo Tudjman, Gojko Susak, and mine, and this was all done in the barracks of the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Just for the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution, the time-frame is 1993. All the documents are relevant to the year 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, sorry for returning to a previous important question. I really try to understand the concatenation of events and also the objectives. No doubt, the documents we saw earlier of March showed that weapons were supplied to the ABiH. One driver from Zenica came to pick them up. This was in March 1993. But I asked you a question then. I asked you whether you knew that the 7th Brigade was stationed in Zenica, and you said, Yes. Therefore, I have to ask you the other side of my question. Did you know that since January 1993, Croatian civilians had been detained in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And despite the fact that they were detained, you send weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, we will see later on when exactly, but it was sometime at the beginning of March. We had a witness here. I was up there in order to calm the situation down. I was in Zenica even with Mr. Prkacin. He was a HOS general, and in some way he was tied to the area, and we tried to see if we could have people released. And I was his driver. At that time, I was a driver in Zenica. Somehow it happened that I was driving Mr. Prkacin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume, then -- with a decision as important as this one, what was the decisive factor to keep on supplying weapons? Was it the fact that you had a common enemy, that is, the Serb forces, and the very fact that there were civilians in Zenica? It was, of course, a dramatic event that could find a solution. Therefore, when you weigh out the common purpose and the issue of civilians detained in Zenica, you ended up opting for the general interest, which was to fight the Serbian forces? Was it that factor that was taken on board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exclusively that element, Your Honour. In war, you never -- or almost never have an opportunity to choose between the good and the evil. In 99 percent of the cases in war, at least this type of war, you have a decision which is bad and a decision which is even worse, and you opt for the lesser evil. You make a decision that you believe will result in less evil. It was painful to talk to the people who were closely related to the detainees over there. However, all of us who were thinking about that, starting with President Tudjman, myself, and Petkovic, what would have happened if we had cut that off and if we had told them, There's no weapons forthcoming? Let's develop that scenario. Bosnia and Herzegovina would simply politically join Yugoslavia, and Muslims would have disappeared. They would have been expelled. 50.000 or 60.000 more people would have been killed. That's at least what the Serbs did. And what good would that have brought us? And a million-plus would have been expelled, and this would have been a total disaster. We never interrupted the supply of weapons, communications means, reproduction materials. Food and humanitarian convoys were the least of our problems. However, Your Honours, of course, listen -- look here, actually. A mother whose son is over there, a man [as interpreted] whose son is detained, she does not want to talk about all things general, she doesn't want to look at the bigger picture. All she cares about is her own detained son. And if you have 50 parents on your hands, the only thought on their minds is that their children are down there, that their children are not coming back. And we, on the other hand, are letting the weapons go through. And that's why the convoy in Citluk was stopped. They were not interested in the global policy of Franjo Tudjman, Petkovic, Stojic, Prlic, or Praljak, or whoever. That mother wants her baby and does not see beyond that, which is only understandable, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, on 3D32-1085, or 3D38-0079, you will see the schematic of the place where the weapons were packaged.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Zdencina and some of the places in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What follows are documents testifying to the way the weapons were packaged. I would like to draw your attention to the screen. It will be easier for you to read, 3D38-0086, and 3D32, is the Croatian version, -1089.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have anything to add to the documents. The documents are self-explanatory. They are clear enough. I just tender those documents for admission. If the Court is going to admit these documents, I have nothing to add to them. They are very clear; they are self-explanatory. Maybe I could answer few questions, and that would bring the whole process to an end. It will probably take me 10 or so minutes to explain everything. If the documents are in, then they speak for themselves. They speak volumes of the time-frame and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's move into private session. Registrar, please, private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, go to the establishment of the units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. The page number is 3D32-1107 in Croatian, and 3D38-0111 in English.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Here, you see that the total number of documents is 158, and they all speak about the establishment of the units, and that in the annex there are 32 documents. And now I'm going to ask you to take us through the annex.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the Croatian version, that's 3D32-1108. We can see a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Let me just give the English reference. It's 3D38-0111.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, where the units that were sent to Central Bosnia were actually set up, the units sent to Bosnia and Posavina and to the Bihac enclave. And here we're talking about units that were made up mostly of ethnic Muslims, and it shows the routes they took.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The units were the 7th Brigade --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 77th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, the 77th. I can hardly see.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The 77th Brigade, the Rijeka, the Berbir Brigade, the Handzar Brigade, and the 17th Brigade from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were their names.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I'm reading.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the next document in Croatian, that's 1109.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have a question to the document 0111. I do not see a date here. Is it possible to have a date?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, 0111, that's an overview, and now as we go through the documents, we'll see the dates. The dates are on the documents. You can see them on the documents. It's 1993 and 1992. This is just an overview, and then through the documents you can see the dates.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's take the next one, then, 1109.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Kovacic -- oh, sorry. I know that in the interest of time, we moved on to 3D38-0111, but you're going to seek to tender all the documents, so this has to be on record. There are documents about July and August, so with regard to the time-frame we have documents about July and August, or even January 1994. Can you confirm this or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Throughout the time, I say that for all those documents that we don't have enough time to go through them. My argument is clear, continually in 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, with minor hitches in the second half of 1993 that we managed to resolve by smuggling the weapons behind our own backs, but the weapons kept coming into Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, follow-up questions about military tactics. I saw in the documents that oil for tanks was supplied, which goes to show that the ABiH had tanks. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The BH Army had quite a few tanks. We gave them a tank from Jablanica, when they wanted to liberate Sarajevo, and then they never -- well, we can't, unfortunately, go through all this. And raw materials for the production of some casings in Konjic. That's what we transported, and there are documents to support it, from the Ploce port, and the materials used for the production of gunpowder. I really -- I'm telling you, boots, clothes, oil, ammunition, telecommunications equipment, raw materials, medicines, well, for the wounded, and the wounded -- it's humanitarian aid, it's not under this chapter. But everything that could be obtained under the conditions went to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the transcript, let me give you the English and Croatian page references for the 7th -- for the July and August of 1993, referring to the consignments going to BH Army. That's 3D32-1099. The English version is 3D38-0099. 3D32-1101, that's the Croatian version; and 3D38-0102, 010 -- oh, I'm sorry, 3201. I'm sorry, I got confused. 3D38-0105, 3D32-1103 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could the shuffles of papers please be kept at a minimum. We can hardly hear the speaker.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... 3D38-0106, that's the English version. 3D32-1104, the Croatian version. 3D32-1105, that's the Croatian version. 3D38-0108, that's the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And now we go back to the establishment of the units, General, but it's also time for our break.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can look at 1109.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Which is, which in English is 3D38-0112.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 26th of January, 1993, and it's the Military Mission of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What's the date?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I gave you the date. It's the 26th of January, Colonel Hasan Efendic, and they are asking for an urgent meeting with General Bobetko. And this is what's on the agenda: To continue discussions and to set up a collection point -- well, in Lika and Kordun they have this collection point centre. That's where Muslims from abroad and from Croatia come. There were quite a few of them living abroad, and then they were to be sent to Bihac because there were some routes still open there. And then item number 2 is a procurement and other -- purchase or other forms of procurement and military equipment; 3, cooperation and coordination between the Croatian Army and the 5th Corps; then maintaining the airlift and various other issues. And this meeting was to be attended by the secretary for military issues from the 5th Corps, Brigadier Hajrudin Osmanagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since it is time for our break, the next document will be dealt with after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Pusic left us for a while. He is not feeling well. We hope that he will come back soon. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, would you open to page 3D32-1110, and the English page is 3D38-0113. It is a report on the work of the Crisis Staff for Bosnia-Herzegovina, Split, dated the 6th of April to the 18th of October, 1992. The document was written in Split, which is the Republic of Croatia, and it was written on the 18th of October, 1992. General, what do you know about the circumstances when this document was compiled, and the work of the Crisis Staff, and the document in general?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me say that there were crisis staffs of this kind for Bosnia-Herzegovina on the territory of the Republic of Croatia in great numbers, and we have a report from Split here and the Crisis Staff in Split. There were many such crisis staffs, and they list how many volunteers they sent to Visoko, to Northern Bosnia, to Krajl Tomislav, which was a unit fighting in Southern Croatia first and then it came under the command of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, that is on 3D 321111 and 3D38-0114. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was saying, the unit came under the direct command later on of Mr. Izetbegovic, and we've already seen this document, and he appointed a commander, and that was the man Daidza, Mate Sarlija - Daidza. And then the 1st Mostar Independent Battalion, that's the battalion that later on became the 1st Mostar Brigade and later on the 4th Corps, with 118 volunteers, and so on and so forth. And in conclusion, they say that they sent over 2.000 volunteers to the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO. And it says that there were women and foreign nationals from Algeria, France, Turkey, who were sent and who helped them; how everybody tried to help them in Split. All the companies and the Croatian Army lent their assistance to these people coming in. Anyway, he explains in detail how much humanitarian aid was being given and how they were generally helped out with transport and in all manner of other ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And the document was signed by the president of the Crisis Staff for Bosnia-Herzegovina, Split, Alija Dzafo; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he is sending this to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it's addressed to them, and to Hasan Efendic, the military attache of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Croatia, and the Bureau of the Republic of BH in Croatia. So the Presidency or Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina had an office in Croatia, bureau in Croatia, and that's where the government meetings were held, and so on and so forth, as they would be in a completely open and friendly country.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: May we have your knowledge and additional information on document 3D32-1112, a document we've already seen, and in English it is 3D38-0123.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 112, but which one? I can't find that 112.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to ask a question with regard to the document which we have just had. It is a report on the work of the Crisis Staff for Bosnia and Herzegovina, Split. I was of the opinion that Split was in Croatia. Now, is this another Split, or how come there is a Bosnia and Herzegovina crisis staff in a Croatian town? Can you explain this, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour Judge Trechsel. That is precisely what I've been talking about all this time; not only in Split, by the way. There were such crisis staffs -- BH crisis staffs in Croatia. Well, certainly more than 10 of them; Split, Rijeka, Zagreb, Sisak, I believe, Slavonski Brod, and so on. As I was saying, Croatia, in all respects, at all levels, at all levels of the army, in every way possible, the government, the president, the authorities, the various towns, offered aid and assistance, comprehensive aid and assistance, to Bosnia-Herzegovina for its defence. And this is one of those reports that says: by providing money, companies, by placing warehouses at their disposal (…) people were collecting too and the weapons were provided. To individuals too, of course. Each of these groups were armed. They didn't go over there bare-handed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm still a bit puzzled. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, I gained the impression that where a crisis staff took over, it took over the functions of the municipal government, as in view of the emergency war situation. I must assume, unless told or explained otherwise, that the term "crisis staff" in Croatian towns does not have the same meaning, but rather is something like an association of the friends of Bosnia-Herzegovina, something of that kind. Is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, partially yes, partially no, Judge Trechsel. The same was done by the crisis staffs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the same things, kind of things, which means that with the siege of Sarajevo and with the state disintegrating and its communications disintegrating, to send anybody to defend something over there and to go up to the front-lines, you had to rally people, collect people from somewhere, collect the weapons, train the people, so this was the same that the crisis staffs in Bosnia-Herzegovina did, the same kinds of activities they were engaged in. These were authorised structures and recognised in the state of Croatia as such, as the military attaches, as branch offices of their Main Staff, in a way. They had their stamp, their papers, their reports, and everything else. So they weren't just a group of friends or an association of friends. They were registered by the Croatian state, recognised by the state. A recognised institution, if you will, by the state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I think that the first sentence in this document explains things. It says that the Crisis Staff for Bosnia-Herzegovina - Split was established as part of the Split branch of the Party of Democratic Action of Croatia. So if I understand things right, the SDA was set up in Croatia. It seems to say this, anyway. And starting from that, a branch of the SDA in Split christened itself "Crisis Staff." Is this how we're supposed to understand this? To your knowledge, was the SDA actually settled in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, the situation was somewhat different. The SDA of Croatia was an independent, autonomous party within Croatia which followed the politics and policies of the SDA of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But it was a party registered in Croatia, just like the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina had the same programme and platform as the HDZ of Croatia, of course, but it was an independent party in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So this was the SDA Party of Croatia, which had its branches, it was registered in Croatia, and on the territory of the Republic of Croatia it existed in this way, as you just read out, and it quite simply organised its legal branch offices. They had their stamps and seals and offices, and everything else. Of course, under normal conditions, in normal countries and circumstances, this activity would not have been permitted, because it would have gone against the grain and letter of many laws, but that's why I keep emphasising that without an overall understanding of the comprehensive situation, it's impossible to understand its individual details in the right way. It was a war. There was a war on. People would lose their lives. Lots of evil had already taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, on page 2, page 114 of the English version, there is one word, and I'm very careful with words and the weight that can be attached to words. It's at the very end of the page, and it says that there were 2.000 volunteers and that through the crisis cell, these volunteers were dispatched to the OSBH and the HVO. So when reading this, it looks like the crisis cell in Split, the BiH Crisis Staff in Split, actually welcomes the volunteers and then decides, on its own volition, how it's going to dispatch these volunteers, which might lead us to think that in the mind of those people in Split, the HVO and the ABiH is just one army, or two armies but joined against a common enemy, against the Serbs. Is this the way it operated, because it seems to be what this document indicates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so, Judge Antonetti. Here you see that these people reported to Pula, Rijeka, Varazdin, and Zadar. They were registered there, and once they had gathered together, there would be a team, and they would say, We're from Mostar, or the surrounding parts, and we would like to go to the Mostar Independent Battalion. Another group would say, We would like to go to Tomislavgrad, and so on. And then that group would be armed and equipped and would be transported to where they wanted to go, to the BH Army and the HVO. And up until this point of time when this document was written, 2.000 volunteers had been recorded and dispatched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is the first time we see this document, but it -- out of memory, I think we've never mentioned this, but it establishes that Muslims in Croatia wanted to go back to Bosnia-Herzegovina and wanted to volunteer, actually, for Bosnia-Herzegovina. So if we have Muslims who volunteer, do you think that it could have had a psychological impact on Croats who said, Well, if Muslims go to Bosnia-Herzegovina, why wouldn't we, as Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina, also go there? Was there, do you think, some kind of impact either in one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at this point in time, Your Honour, nothing. At this point in time, the feeling of a joint struggle was complete, so during this period there were no thoughts if the Muslims were to go and so on. It was all on a volunteer basis, according to individual sentiments, whether Croats or Muslims, and they felt this urge, basic urge, inner urge to go, a moral duty to go and defend areas where they thought were necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document dates October 18, 1992, and this is around the Prozor elements. When the incidents occurred in Prozor, I assume that in Croatia people knew about what had happened in Prozor through the Muslims who were volunteering to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina, to be dispatched within the ranks of the HVO or of the ABiH. As far as you know, could you tell us whether the incidents in Prozor were actually relayed in the Croatian press, and do you believe that these incidents had an impact on the behaviour of the volunteers to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer is yes. There were reports about that in the press, and this was considered a conflict of local significance. To your second question, Your Honour, not in general terms, but there may have been individuals who hailed from the area were impacted by the conflict, but in global terms that influence did not exist. And another thing that you can see in the document is that what the Croatian Army did was also done by Croatian companies. Towards the end of the third page in Croatian, it says that the Laucevic company and the ship-building yards and all the volunteers and employees of those companies were still on their payroll and that the salaries were received by their families, upon our approval. As I said, a lot of people in Bosnia and Herzegovina worked in those companies, because the constructor and the ship-building yards were big companies. These people were still on their payrolls, and the money went to their families, which had already been refugees or residing in the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thanks to your answer, I can top this off and discuss this essential question of Prozor. We know that you were there. We've had witnesses on this, and I'm sure you'll come back to this. But when you were in Prozor, when you were over there, did you go on your own volition, because you said, Well, there's a local incident that occurred, let me go to try and cool things down over there? Or did Mr. Tudjman tell you, Slobodan, go there. You have to go; a local incident just occurred. It might completely disrupt the situation, and you need to go over there and do something about it? As far as you remember, could you tell us how it happened? Remember that you're under oath, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am aware of that. I was aware of that from the very beginning, Your Honour. I spoke about that yesterday, and today I'm going to provide some more detail. There are two events. One concerns Prozor, and the other concerns Uskoplje -- Vakuf, yes. Both times, before I went up there, I first had a word with President Tudjman. At one of the meetings with President Tudjman, there was also President Alija Izetbegovic. With the best of intentions, I got mixed up, I don’t know whether this was before going to Rama, but it is probably before I went to Uskoplje, Gornji Vakuf. But it doesn't really matter; it's neither here nor there. However, what does matter is the fact that at one of these -- or, rather, both times, I was asked to go there and try and calm the situation down, stop the conflict, and try to put things in order. Both times, and I don't know at which Mr. Alija Izetbegovic was present, on one of the two occasions, and I don't know which one that was, and I said that, Mr. Franjo Tudjman, the president of the Croatian state, said that to me in the following way: Praljak, this obviously cannot be recorded. There is a difference between the spoken word and the written word. He was slamming his fist on the desk, and he said, Slobodan, go there. We don't want war with the Muslims. Stop it, stop it. Of course, I obeyed him. This was not an order. He could not issue an order to me. This was a request, which I obviously would not have turned down. And then I did it in cooperation with Stojic, Petkovic, and the rest of the team down there. However, I'm going to tell you exactly how all that transpired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is why I said that you'll probably come back to this at one point in time, but I think it's important to keep all this in mind. Madam Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Following up on the questions about this document, General, according to what you know, the SDA of Croatia, was it active in 1993 and 1994 in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It still exists to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: At the time that the indictment refers to in 1993 and 1994, was there ever a ban on its work?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Since we are talking about Prozor, and when you were answering questions by His Honour Judge Antonetti about your departure to Prozor in 1992, in October and later on, the question that imposes itself is as follows: Why did President Tudjman and, on one occasion, President Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic, why did they ask you to go down there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is much more probable that on the 15th of January, Mr. Izetbegovic was there when they asked me to go to Uskoplje. This is a much more probable scenario. I was in the territory of South-East Herzegovina. I was in command down there, and I believe that the witnesses who have testified in this courtroom, and all the others, demonstrated and showed they trusted me and that both the peoples trusted me, the representatives of both the peoples trusted me. I believe, and I will later show, that I did my job with a maximum degree of correctness, energy and involvement. And then until the very end of the conflict, before they pinned the bridge on me, I was held in high esteem by the commanders of both militaries, and you will see that in Travnik too, and so on. And the soldiers. If there's anything I can say about myself, this would be it. And I believe that this was testified by the Muslims who have testified here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you now please open page 3D32-1122. English, 3D38-0123. This is a list of the members of the 77th Brigade. Could you say something about the 77th Brigade? The document was issued by Rijeka Municipality, and the entire document is voluminous and is in e-court under 3D022259 [as interpreted]. And it contains the handwriting of all the listed -- 3D02259.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
