utterances.text: You've already spoken. You said something yesterday, when we were discussing the issues of Hrvatski Vojnik."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are 664 men. That's the last number, 664. There's a list of all the men here. And as I already said, most of them are Muslims. There is nothing to add to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The following document is 3D32-1115, and the English version is 3D38-0124. This is the Crisis Staff for Bosnia-Herzegovina in Split again. The year is 1992. The number is 3D32-1125. This is the number of the Croatian document. Do you want to say something about the document or is this just one in the series of documents issued by the Crisis Staff in Split?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did, we did manage to gather those in Split, and those are always the same documents, where it says that it -- that a war crime is being committed and that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and home- grown Bosniaks in Split should work, they made the decision to continue with their activity and in the just struggle and that this work is immeasurable for the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mehmed Malkoc is hereby appointed, and the military attache is going to be informed about that These are the offices of the military attaches of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Croatia, and this is under his jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This document has a comment that follows the decision on the second page, and the page is 3D32-1126; English, 3D38-0126. It was issued on the 28th of December, 1993, in Split.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is self-explanatory. I really don't know, what else I could say? Again, they were commended by the commission of the Croatian SDA, within that framework, and it says that the military delegation of the BiH Army, consisting of Colonel Rifat Bilajac, Bina [phoen] Fabijan, and Said Rizvic, and from all the military and civilian authorities in Split are thanked for having helped to defend the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It says that there were volunteers that would help Bosnia and Herzegovina, and their only desire was for their homeland of Bosnia-Herzegovina to be saved. And it says here since this is all about military issues and matters, all this information should be preserved and kept safe from unauthorised persons. In those areas, there was a limitless number of spies from all states, from the KOS, the former State Security Service, and the international community sent a huge number of those who did whatever they did in each of their contingents, and that's why this has to be preserved and kept safe in order to protect the members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Go to 3D32-1132; English, 3D38-0133. The document bears the date the 29 October, 1992. It was based on the decision of the Presidency of the Republic of -- the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on general mobilisation. What I would like to draw your attention to is the text below the order. General, do you know anything about the armed forces of the HV under the command of Senad Dedic a member of the HV for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, yes; that's this. These people have to be transported to Mount Igman, close to Sarajevo, the Famos Hotel by bus. They once again have to take the long and hard road. Among them is Christopher James Watson, who is an Englishman, and again military attache is signed, and it's very difficult to understand, it's very difficult to accept that. However, in a speech of his, Franjo Tudjman said, and we saw the speech yesterday, he said that they behaved in the Republic of Croatia as they would have -- I don't know whether they would have be served [as interpreted] in the same way in their own state. They were free. I'm not saying that we knew all that. However, they were free to do whatever they wanted. They could issue orders. They received everything they ever wanted. They would come armed, they would leave armed. In that sense, in that sense, we did not behave as a different state. We behaved as their own branch office for everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And, General, what about Igman? Why is Mount Igman important?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did it have any bearing on the issue of Sarajevo and the defence of Sarajevo and other areas?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the only possible passage through which you could enter Sarajevo and then later on via the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please go to 3D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You are overlapping, you start speaking while the interpretation is going on, so perhaps you could start again.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, 3D32-1135 is the next page I would like you to look at; English, 3D38-0136. This is a document about the mobilisation of the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was sent to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia and the Police Administration of the city of Zagreb. Do you have any personal knowledge about the circumstances surrounding this document, i.e., about the need to mobilise people and how the mobilisation was implemented?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with what I have been repeating, without any reason to repeat things, he says that one of the three officials of the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is in Zagreb, and those are Dr. Semso Tankovic, Tomo Krsticevic, and Miljenko Brkic. It says that there are some problems; they're talking about the rights to stamp documents, who is an authorised person, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the beginning, where it says: "Certain problems and misunderstandings have occurred in recent times when taking in and deporting military conscripts for -- who are the citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and who are currently staying in the Republic of Croatia, a task being carried out by the Ministry of the Interior as instructed --"

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a misunderstanding at stake here. They had proclaimed mobilisation, and they wanted people who were to respond to the mobilisation. They asked for these people to be taken in. And from that arose some problems because there were people who didn't want to go, and they cited their right not to go into war, and the Red Cross approved that because one can refuse to go into war. And when the legal dimension of the problem was finally understood, then this whole exercise was abandoned. However, they thought --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could the general indicate whether this is a document from 1992 or 1993. It says "23 September," but the year is not indicated. It's not on the original, either. We looked at that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer that question, but it is more likely that this was the year 1992 because the mobilisation was declared at that time, and it's more likely that it's 1992 than 1993, and I think that Dr. Semso Tankovic was -- I don't know -- he was the president of the SDA in Zagreb, or if not, he was a high-ranking member of the organisation. And Dr. Semso Tankovic teaches at the School of Economics in Zagreb, and he's a member of the Croatian Parliament today. I think he's serving his second or third term of office. He lived in Croatia, he's a Croatian citizen, and he was also a member of the BH government. So anything went. When it came to assisting the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, all legal provisions of law or intensity of law or rank could be violated; who was born where, who was a member of what government. So he could, at the same time, serve as a member of the government and, at the same time, teach at the Zagreb School of Economics, and -- THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me, from what I was able to understand from the interpretation, I think that General Praljak said that it was the citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina residing in the Republic of Croatia that were being drafted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's what I said, conscripts, citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina who are in -- well, I know from my own job that there were problems, because this was not supposed to be done, because you cannot draft --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're talking about people being brought in.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, but it was on the demand of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not the decision of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I'm sorry, yes, that's all correct. But soon enough, people realised that this could not be done, that there could be no mobilisation in the territory of another state.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could we now move to our next topic, and the topic is the training centres of the BH Army in the Republic of Croatia. That's at page 3D32-1140; English, 3D38-0140. The total number of documents that we have, regarding the training centres, is 120, and in this file we have 15 of them. General, what can you tell us, in general? What is your personal knowledge about the existence of the BH Army training centres in the Republic of Croatia? And then we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of the locations where training centres are listed here --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That's at page 3D32-1142; English, 3D38-0141. In e-court, the map is much more visible than it is in the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here are the training centres, training -- well, no, these are not pilots.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: No, these are not pilots. The training for BH Army members in 1991-1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we have a wrong map on the e-court. It was in Borongaj, as far as Zagreb was concerned, then in Svete Simonska [phoen] Street at Sljeme --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could the speakers not speak at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to correct the number for the sake of e-court. It's 3D32-1142.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Wait for each other. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It would really be helpful if the Judges would not have to recall this rule all the time. Is it not possible to make an effort and to refrain from this shooting before the other shot has arrived, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to restrain myself. 3D32-1141. Now we have the right map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, here we have a list of locations in Croatia where there were training centres, where BH Army personnel were trained. There are two, four, six, eight, ten, twelve -- twelve. These are not all of them, but I listed just the major ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Do you have anything else?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Anything apart from this on the training centres?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from that, not. Ms. Pinter, training centres are training centres. People are gathered there, and then they're trained for combat before being sent to Bosnia and Herzegovina, to the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please open 3D32-1144. That's the Croatian version, 3D38-0144. And the next page, that's the list of candidates for specialist training in the Croatian MUP. The document was issued by the Democratic Action Party of Sarajevo. The date is the 8th of July, 1991, and there is a list of documents -- or, rather, of persons who underwent this training, and the last number is 463.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From this document, we can see that in the Democratic Action Party, there was somebody who was smart when it came to police. At that time, I think it was Delimustafic, and Stojic was also in the ministry, and they were smart enough to realise that -- to realise what was in the offing. And then through the party, because at that time they couldn't do it through the state because it would naturally cause a total hysteria among the Serbs, so they went through the party channels, seeking assistance from Croatia in the training of these people. Of course, war was already raging in Croatia, but Croatia did admit those people and I think they spent seven days, yes, seven days in a training course, and then they went back. And I think that at the beginning, the Special Police played an important role in saving Sarajevo, Vikic's units, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. Here we have a document of the 3rd of August, 1992, at page 3D32-1147, and the English version is 3D38-0146. A mention is made of a Handzar division. Do you know anything about the Handzar Division, where it was established, and where it fought, and in what theaters?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it is not a division. That was its name, the Handzar Division, but it was a unit, a small brigade, half a brigade, in terms of its strength. It fought in Posavina. It gathered in the Republic of Croatia, and it was trained in the Republic of Croatia. These -- this kind of authorisations were issued by all the commanders. They would provide them with a piece of paper that was then used by the gentleman in question by way of introduction in Croatia. All the clubs gathering people who originated from certain areas, there were dozens of them in Croatia, were people from Visoko, Brcko, Tuzla, Doboj would gather. Those were the so-called home clubs, and then they would gather aid only for their specific location. So it was parallel activities. It was done on all levels and parallel efforts, because everybody wanted to do something. So every commander from Bosnia and Herzegovina, either from the HVO or from the BH Army, would get some kind of an authorisation in order to be able to maybe find something to purchase in addition to the official channels, maybe some people they knew in Germany, and then they would go to East Germany and buy army surplus stuff left after Russian -- after Russians withdrew, because people were really clever. So there were thousands and thousands of these kinds of papers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I was waiting for the transcript to finish. Could you please now turn -- now we're going to the file about the training of pilots from Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia. This file begins at page 3D32-1156, and the English version begins at 3D38-0155, generally speaking, about the training of pilots from Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in all other areas, they couldn't do it in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Croatia provided not only the knowledge of its own pilots and the capabilities at its disposal to train the pilots, helicopter pilots and -- well, for the most part, they didn't have any planes. But the pilots who knew how to fly planes had to now be retrained to fly helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could you please now look at page 3D32-1159.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't have 58?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I do. I'm sorry. Very well. So could we first look at 3D32-1158. That's 3D38-0157 in the English version. The date is the 9th of August, 1992, Sarajevo, the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the president, Alija Izetbegovic, the minister of national defence, Jerko Doko, sends to the Ministry of the National Defence of the Republic of Croatia its request. What do you know, General, about this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here we have the first 22 people, so this is the 9th of August, 1992. The war is raging. Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, as the president of the Presidency, and Minister Jerko Doko signed this request. And, of course, this was complied with, Croatia provided those services. And the people listed here were sent to appropriate training, as requested. The only thing that's wrong here is we didn't have the Ministry of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Our next document is the one that I referred to earlier. That's 3D32-1159, and the English version is 3D38-0159. This is the document dated the 27th of December, 1992. Again, this is the training of pilots and technicians in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As Judge Antonetti would say, after the conflicts in Rama and some conflicts in Novi Travnik, well, the conflicts did not change anything in terms of the political and all other decisions in the Republic of Croatia, the commitment to help Bosnia-Herzegovina in every way, in every way. I mean every way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: There was training in 1993. We can see that from the document 3D32-1161; English, 3D38-0162. Do you want to say something about this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says here arrangements have been made with the command of the air force and air defence of the Republic of Croatia. Of course, they couldn't talk to the air force without an appropriate decision of Minister Susak and without my decision, because at that time I was involved in the political decision-making, and, of course, without the appropriate decision of Franjo Tudjman. They couldn't just go there and do that without any political decision made by the political leadership. And we are now on the 8th of March, 1993. Nothing has changed in the policy of the Republic of Croatia, and nothing will change in the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, and negotiations are underway. On the 3rd of March, there were negotiations in New York.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. As far as the political relations are concerned, Alija Izetbegovic has already trampled on lots of things; Cutileiro's Plan; the Vance-Owen Plan was also set aside; the elements of the behavior and where it was all going. It was clear to people who didn't have such sharp political eyesight. But still we didn't change our policies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I'm looking at this document as I was looking at the others. This morning I was reading your pre-trial brief in which you were speaking of the international armed conflict. As far as you know, and you have read a lot, you have studied a lot, in the history of armies can we find situations in which there is a conflict between a state, say State A and State B, in which the State B would get their pilots trained in the other state? Has such a situation occurred yet, as say, for example, today in Afghanistan, as if NATO were to train Taliban pilots or soldiers? Do you have any such examples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I said already, and I maintain this, and I challenge any military expert to contest my claims. The way that the Republic of Croatia acted towards the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Muslims, at an earlier stage when there were isolated, small-scale conflicts, and later on when there were major conflicts, especially in Konjic in Central Bosnia, and then further down to Mostar, the policy remained the same almost as if nothing was going on there. There is no precedent in history, no such example in history, anything of the sort where a state and a nation acted in this manner towards another state, towards Muslims, even at the time -- this is what they said loud and clear. Even at the time when those people attacked elements of that same nation. Just imagine, what would happen if someone were to attack the French in Quebec. Let's say that the English -- anglophone-Canadians, for instance, and then France is arming and aiding the English who are attacking the French in Quebec. Well, that has never happened anywhere else. Let me give you an example from the Second World War, when de Gaulle approved the air-strikes by the English in which lots of French soldiers were killed, because the French officers refused to hand over the shipping to the English because some of the French officers hated the English more than they hated Hitler, but that was dictated by the logic of war. This is contrary -- this, what we have here, is contrary to any logic of war. You can call any of your generals and ask them whether they would do anything of the sort and whether they heard of anything of the sort. And now in some heads we are presented as members of a joint criminal enterprise, and this is absurd. But as a man said, if it is absurd, then it cannot be refuted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, we have heard not very, very much, but some about the actual fighting between HVO and ABiH. Can you tell the Chamber to what extent and at what moment the ABiH attacked the HVO by planes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that the BH Army attacked by planes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I did not say that you said it. I ask you whether you know about this. You say no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is a problem of interpretation, and it is in the transcript, so it is a short-circuit here, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army had helicopters, Judge Trechsel, and it released some explosive devices that way and transferred some of its units in Operation 93, and transferred its units and its commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sure we will hear more about this. Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, in the transcript it was recorded that it was Operation 93. What operation did you mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neretva-93, I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The next document is 3D32-1163, and the English, 3D38-0164. The document is dated the 24th of July, 1992. It is signed by Petar Stipetic, the deputy chief of the Main Staff of the HVO for the combat sector, and the document relates to retraining. The document has a handwritten addition, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Stipetic sent this to the minister of defence, and the defence minister says, Let Praljak decide. And this is Ms. Zloic's [phoen] handwriting, Mr. Susak's secretary. So I was informed about things like this, and we made our decisions jointly, but you didn't need to think much about it because there was a general position that had been taken, and we just confirmed it, and that it should be continued.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: In the document, it says that it refers to pilots who, on BH territory, would fly for the defence of that republic. And this assignment was urgent because of the constant need for evacuation and supplies for the Territorial Defence of BiH. So can you tell us why you had this authorisation standing agreement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, the next document is 3D32-1170, and the English is 3D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to decipher this document. You're giving the go-ahead for three pilots and technicians to come, but did they fly? Did they come by plane?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how they arrived, but they were retrained to fly Antonov-2 type planes, and those planes, well, I don't know whether they purchased one somewhere, but it was the Croatian Air Force that had these freight planes. They're not too big, this type of plane, the Antonov-2. And they mostly flew from Pleso Airport in Zagreb towards the airports that were operational at that time. One was in Coralic, at Bihac. Then there was Tuzla. I know about those two for certain, but I wouldn't like to hazard a guess about the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are saying that these Antonovs took off from the Zagreb Airport, and they went to Tuzla, Bihac, Coralic and so on. But did they also do the return trip? Did they also take off from Tuzla, Bihac, in order to go to Zagreb and land in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We would load them up with everything that was required over there; weapons, medical corps material, cigarettes, which are very important in a war, and then they would bring in the wounded over there, and some women and children, or anybody who is sick, and people who the staff had designated as needing to go back to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us whether these Antonovs were flown by Muslim pilots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were both; a lot of Croatian pilots, too, who also flew those planes for the requirements and needs of the BH Army. Now, Your Honours, mostly they would fly by night, with their light switched off, and they would come into contact with the airport -- well, they would contact the airport just before landing, and then the lights would be quickly switched on. This was all at night. They would land quickly, unload quickly, reload quickly, and fly off, because of course the Serbs targeted the planes, and there were planes that had been shot down.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, following on from Judge Antonetti's question, I'd like to take you back to page 3D32-1161, or in English, 3D38-0162. And I'd like to look at item 2, which speaks about training on the AN-2 type plane, which we have heard is the Antonov plane. So can you tell us the names of the people listed here? Are those Muslim names, Bosniak names, or are they Croats?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from this man Ante Grigic, the rest are all Muslims. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now turn the page -- or, rather, turn to 3D32-1170, and the English is 3D38-0173. The document is dated the 4th of January, 1993, and it is addressed to Major General Imra Agotic, who was the commander of the Croatian Air Force and Air Defence, and the document is signed by Josip Hrgovic [phoen], and it relates to cargo transport from Coralic Airport. Does this document confirm -- or, rather, would you agree that this document 8 confirms all the things you've told us so far? Have you got anything to add?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just to say that at the end of the year, they drew up a review of what they did. And they said that for the requirements of BiH, there were six flights; and for the TO of BiH, there were twenty-eight flights, sorties, and all the other data mentioned, including the pilots. And then it says at the end that there were 280 flights in the period gone by, 71 over-flight hours. And it says that on the territory of Croatia, 118 passengers were transported and 46 wounded. So that's what I said. That was the purpose of it, to take weapons to them over there and to bring back these people and also BH Army officials, the wounded, or whoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: For the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. Could the general indicate perhaps on the map the locations where these materials were going to, because the font that's used in the English transcript, I can't -- I'm not sure that I can read the name of the airport, and perhaps he could just indicate where Kazin [phoen] or Cazin is located.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's by Bihac, the airport by Bihac, and Tuzla is over here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: For the transcript, General, let's just state that the document gives a recapitulation summary of transportation for the needs of BiH and for the TO of BiH. And on page 2 of the document we have the names of the crew carrying out the flights and the number of flight hours.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Fine. Now let's move on to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in this document we see that wounded are being transported. I would like to know whether, among these wounded, there are ABiH soldiers, soldiers who were wounded and who are going to be flown to Croatia to be treated in Croatian hospitals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, never -- never, ever, did we look to see who the wounded were. There were far more BH Army wounded than HVO wounded, because there were far more BH soldiers than there were HVO soldiers. And all those who were transported to the Republic of Croatia, all the ones that we could admit and take in, and we'll see later on that it was more than 10.000 people, we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm putting this question to you because I'm trying logically to reintegrate this in this notion of international armed conflict. This document establishes that there were flights between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it also establishes that wounded were flown during these flights, and you're telling us that, according to you, as far as you were concerned, you made no difference between ABiH soldiers and HVO soldiers. However, if ABiH soldiers are wounded, and had been actually wounded by HVO soldiers in the framework of a local conflict, would it be -- is it logical for them to be -- it is logical that they would be sent back to be treated. But if it's an international conflict, is it logical to have Country A to take care of the wounded of the other side that is opposed to it, in an international armed struggle? What can you say about all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The war doctrine which was developed over a period of time required the following: that the ammunition to put the opposite side out of action should be done in such a way that there would be far more wounded than killed, because it was considered that a wounded soldier inflicted far greater damage on the enemy side than did a dead soldier. First of all, you have to take them away from the battle-front, which requires additional men. Then costly treatment is required and so on. So modern ammunition was developed to that effect. The Croatian Defence Council, and I personally, and you've already heard this from me, Your Honours, we never -- well, whatever the wounded -- whoever the wounded person was, be he from the BH Army, if we were able to, we would take in the wounded, and you saw this with the example of Mostar. We would always give them aid and assistance. And we heard the testimony here from -- testimony here from SpaBat from August and September of 1993, and I personally took part in that. That is to say, we took in four groups, transported them or that family from Rama. I took them in. Not only did they go to Split, but I also asked that they be granted Croatian citizenship, which they did receive, and so they used the social insurance of the state of Croatia. It paid for them to go to Switzerland. And the Judge said that he knew full well how much medical treatment costs, what medical treatment costs in Switzerland. So not only did we differentiate between the different people, but the BH Army wounded were taken care of in Croatia, given medical treatment in Croatia. And you saw that I used a helicopter on one occasion, and I never flew in a helicopter; not because I was afraid, but because the occasion didn't arise. Anyway, I transported a Muslim lady doctor from Mostar. Unfortunately, she died, but we did our best to save her. And there were dozens of examples like that. So never, ever did we make any distinction between people, and we invested great efforts to cater to everyone. And you have seen evidence of that many a time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now we're going to show a document relating to the Silajdzic family who was transported from Prozor to Split and from there to Switzerland. We have those documents, and we will be presenting them in court, but they haven't been included into this particular book and edition.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me say that I never spoke about this in public until I saw the indictment, because I'm ashamed to speak of things like that. The fact that they forced me to talk about this, I feel shame for having done so. May I have a break, please? May we have a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a 20-minute break, and we will resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. I have a request to make with Mr. Kovacic. Paragraph 52 of your pre-trial brief, you mentioned a joint statement made by Tudjman and Izetbegovic on September 14th, 1993. And according to this statement, it says, and I quote: "Conflicts among the units of the ABiH and the HVO." And in the footnote, you referred to the Exhibit D50 in the Kordic case. I would like to know exactly what is the exact number of this statement. I believe that it must have been already integrated into your evidence list.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the statement has a 3D number. It's already in evidence. General Praljak's Defence team wants to talk about that statement when we come to the year 1993, since therefore we have been following a certain chronology of events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, so I'll keep this in mind. Let's resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, please go to 3D32-1173. In English, it is 3D38-0176. The annex refers to the logistical centres of the BH Army which were established in the Republic of Croatia. The number of documents -- the total number of documents in the possession of the Defence is 834, and the annex contains a total of 41 documents about that subject. The following document I would like to discuss is 3D32-1174, and in English it is 3D38-0177. The date on the document is 12 July 1993. The document was signed by the deputy minister of the government in Bosnia and Herzegovina. General, could you please tell us what you know about the document and what --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you again have some crystal-clear documents in front of you. The conflict already is underway, on the 12th of July there was a conflict, and I'm always going to call it the attack of the BH Army in Central Bosnia. This was after the 30th of June and the incidents in Mostar, after the events that took place in Mostar on the 9th of May, after the events in Konjic and so on and so forth. We're talking about the 12th of July, 1993, and here the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina says that it issued a decision in order to perform duties and tasks from the framework of activities of the Staff of the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina outside the territory of the republic itself, and the following persons are appointed. In the Military and Economic Representative Office in Zagreb, six persons are mentioned here within the Logistical Department of the Supreme Command Staff of the Armed Forces in Zagreb, so in addition to the Economic Representative Office, there is also the Logistics of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and what follows are 21 members. And then the Logistical Department of the Staff of the Supreme Command in Split counts two members. These people, after having been appointed, will represent the permanent staff in the logistical departments for as long as there is a need for them being there. There is also a statement of reasons, which says that the Staff of the Supreme Command issued a request to issue accreditations to the logistical centres of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. A request was for them to be able to do all of that. The war was already underway. We're talking about the year 1993, and the conflict had been on since 1992. And the military force that we are in conflict with appoints its members a whole staff. It's not a part of the state bodies of foreign affairs, it's a staff. I really can't say anything more about that. I believe this is perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see what the policy of the Croatian state was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Trial Chamber's information, this document that the general has just spoken about is in e-court under 3D00302, and it's already been admitted. And as regards the document about which Judge Antonetti asked the witness about, a joint statement issued in September 1993, issued by Dr. Franjo Tudjman and Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, this is also an exhibit bearing the following number: P05051. 5051, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, could you please go to 3D32-1176. In English, it is 3D38-0180. The document was drafted on the 15th of July, 1993, by the Embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb, and the document was sent to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Croatia. What can you tell us about this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the 15th of July, 1993, and they say, You, in Croatia, and your Ministry of Foreign Affairs, please convey the information. They are asking the information on their appointment in the territory of the Republic of Croatia in the logistical departments to be conveyed to Croatia, to the HVO. It says here that a certain number of persons have been appointed. The persons in question are listed in the document. It says that their stay will be regulated in keeping with the regulations of the Republic of Croatia. Well, now, I am not sure that a foreign military force is allowed to have their bases in the Republic of Croatia. There's no law in Croatia allowing that, and it's nonsense, but they perceived Croatia as a prolonged hand of their own state, because that's what we had allowed them. Of all these names, only Blanko Vucak is not Muslim. All the others are Muslim. And at the end, they say, very properly, that the Embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina takes the opportunity to express their sentiment of deepest respect to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Croatia. All this was possible and functioned for as long as they deemed it necessary, not because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, could you please try to be more concise in your answers and try to refrain from making comments or going a bit overboard. Otherwise, it's a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything is clear. If it's clear, it's clear; if it's not, it's not. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I would like to state for the record where were the logistical centres in the Republic of Croatia, because the document is not clear. I would like to say that there were two; one in Zagreb and one in Split. The following document I would like you to look at is on page 3D32-1179.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 78 says that they received salaries, that they were working, that these men were working -- or these people, rather, and receiving salaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This is the document on page 3D38-0182 in English, and in Croatian it is 3D32-1178.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, here you have it. It says here that the military officers received salaries for the month of July 1993. The monies are specified here, which means that they were working at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What's the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Number 3D32-1179; English, 3D38-0184. The date is 6 August 1993. That's on the document. And the document was issued by the Embassy of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia. The military mission issued the document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the money that they spent after having been received from Mr. Hasan Cengic, who was the main logistician of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. In order to gain some time, General, which documents in the bundle about the logistical centres would you like to draw our attention to? I believe that it would be necessary for us to pay attention to document 3D32-1185. This is a report on the work, dated 29 April 1993, by the Military Mission. It's not very legible in my copy. Could you please look at your copy. The English page is 3D38-0194.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 29th of April, 1993, the document was issued. It's a rather long. I would not like to waste anybody's time. In the document, they explain what they do, who they negotiated with and how. And again the document testifies about the basic thesis, which is very clear. And I don't really have anything to say unless specifically asked to answer questions. I don't want to waste any more time providing explanations about the things that have already been explained thoroughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The document also provides the chronology of the development of the Military Mission and tasks that it had. And the following document I would like you to look at is on page 3D32-1191. In English, it is 3D38-0199, 38-0199. The date is 7 March 1993.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, once again we can ask the question in this manner: How can somebody from the 2nd Corps, from Tuzla, can issue the authorisation to Fadil Muhic, who is a member of the BH Army, because he is under the command as the Deputy Commander of the corps testified here, authorising him to purchase weapons and other items necessary for the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to enter into contracts and take all other action without any restrictions in the territories of the republics of Croatia and Slovenia, and these authorisation is valid for those two states. Well, I would like somebody could come with a paper from Switzerland, or France, or Hungary, waving this piece of paper, saying, Well, I can do pretty much as I please, because this has the signature of somebody from the 2nd Corps. But at that time, this was a normal occurrence in our circumstances and because of our efforts to provide assistance. This is what this man was doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. We will be skipping documents from 1992. Let us look at the document from 1993. It's at page 3D32-1198. The English version is 3D38-0206.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we skipped, Ms. Pinter, the lists of people who were in the Logistics Base of the Supreme Command Staff of the BH Army in Samobor, and then you can see how many people there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I skipped because my colleague, Ms. Nozica, used it as 2D00498, but you can say something about this document. It's at page 3D32-1194. The English version is 3D38-0203.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is just to show to the Judges that in the Logistics Centre in Sarajevo -- Sarajevo [as interpreted] is a small place, it's too small to be on the map. It's Samobor, and you can see how many people worked there, the payroll expenses. Well, I don't want to go into that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. The name of the place is Samobor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I would now like to take you back to 3D32-1198 in Croatian, 3D38-0206 in English. The date is the 10th of September, 1993. It's an association -- okay, are you going to tell us about this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Jankomir, it's on the outskirts of Zagreb. There are some warehouses there. It's warehouse number 8. This is where goods of the BH Army, uniforms, boots, and so on, are stored. And about 30.000 items, worth approximately 20 million German marks. That was the assessment at the time. And the Croatian MUP -- well, Your Honours, at that time there was a flourishing black market. You know that when you're dealing with such huge amounts of money, and volumes of procurement, there are people who are dishonest, who don't do their in an honest manner, and then there's smuggling, and at that time some of the representatives of the logistics bases started buying weapons on the black market from Croatian soldiers who had bought their weapons from some other sources or who had been demobilised. So there was a subversive activity, so to speak, in this area, and the Croatian MUP was actually trying to put some order into all that. And the only demand there is for a person to show up with the appropriate accreditation and immunity, who would be the representative of the BH Embassy and to sign as the owner, because the goods would be removed and somebody would smuggle the goods. It is not in dispute that this quantity of goods worth 20 million German marks should be transferred to BH. But at that time there were quite a few people in Croatia who were trying to profit from this whole effort. But this is the 10th of September, and in the warehouse there are 30.000 pieces of each of these items, three corps of the army. That's much more than I had, or General Petkovic before me, under our command in terms of the troops, number of troops; effective command, not including those who were in the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Let us move on to 3D32-1206; it's 3D38-0214 in the English version, because we're only using documents from 1993. Well, this is Alija Izetbegovic's handwriting. We are already familiar with it. It's a certificate written on paper with the Hilton Hotel letterhead. It was signed in Vienna, confirming that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic -- well, I can't really see the name in the hard copy, but it should be Fatih --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alhamnej.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, I can't read it. And the amount is listed here. At that time, were you aware that Mr. Izetbegovic -- rather, that the leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina were receiving aid from outside, from other persons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we knew that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You knew that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we knew that there was a lot of this aid. It was huge amounts. And according to the information that was published in the BH press, the aid was to the amount of several billion German marks, and the HVO did not receive a single German mark. This was aid not to the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but to the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The next document on the next page confirms what we've just said, but let me just quote it for the record. 3D32-1207 and 3D38-0215. And I think I have to intervene. There is an error in interpretation. In the English language -- or, rather, in translation, it says "300.000 German marks," and it should actually read "60.000 German marks." We have this document, 3D32-1208. The English number is --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We'll skip that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's move on to that -- to the document of the 14th of September, 1993, to see who paid what.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It is the document that is 3D32-1212, that's the Croatian version, and the English version is 3D38-0218. The document is the 7th of December --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's actually the 14th of September, Ms. Pinter. What the document dated the 7th -- which number did you say?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the document dated the 14th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, but there is another page. It was a translation that was done on the 7th of December, 1993, because it's German; it's in the German language.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The translation, Ms. Pinter, was done as part of an investigation conducted by the German authorities that -- and Austrian -- or, rather, Austrian and German authorities that started addressing the problem of those huge transfers of money, and for the most part that was cash, and it went through this organisation TWRA. Those amounts were paid to Hasan Cengic and Alija Izetbegovic, to Muslims. Let me be loud and clear. This was paid to the Muslims by the Islamic countries. And there was a large-scale investigation in Germany and Austria regarding this problem. And in this document, you can see that the meeting was held in the President Hotel in Geneva. And, of course, there were no Croats present. It was Izetbegovic, Ganic, Silajdzic, and Mr. El Fatah Hussein [phoen], who was the director of the TWRA organisation. And here they say that they will set up a bank and how they would assist Preporod and the organisation of -- that helps the families of the Sahid. All the Muslims who are killed for the cause are considered as Sahid, although the Sahid are not those who are killed in the defence of the state, but in the defence of Islamic teachings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: For the record, the Prosecution is going to object to this document, as well as the previous one, which was on page 214 of the English. We appear to be moving into a different area. It's sort of interesting, but it's not relevant; that is, activities of the Muslim or the Bosnia-Herzegovina leadership to arm themselves. There are some transactions that are referred to here taking place outside of Croatia in Vienna. So we don't appear to be, at least for these last two documents, talking about Croatia's involvement or assistance or support in the efforts of the Bosnian-Herzegovina government to acquire arms. And so I think these last couple of documents are irrelevant for those reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me respond to my learned friend Mr. Stringer. This document pertains to Alija Izetbegovic, the president of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading from the document, where it says "President of the Republic." Then there is Ejup Ganic, the vice-president of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Haris Silajdzic, foreign minister in the government. So if we're talking about the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina and if these are the highest officials, representatives of that state, and there are no Croats among them, and there are no political representatives of the Croatian people, and indeed they are unaware of all this, and if we link this with the allegations in the indictment, then this is a highly relevant document showing that there was a double policy on the other side, while Croatia was giving as much as it could to assist Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the other hand, representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the indictment alleges that Croats and the HZ-HB ignored them and bypassed them, are not only collecting money, but they're travelling around purporting to be representing Bosnia-Herzegovina, never saying that this was a state in which Croats and Serbs also lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may supplement as well, because I think it goes to the heart of the joint criminal enterprise and it also goes to the heart of our theory of the Defence, part of which was brought in, as you may recall, through one of our very last witnesses. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Mr. Karnavas. On what capacity are you now taking the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, we have been charged with joint criminal enterprise. We moved to sever from this case so we could be tried separately. We did it before the trial; we did it during the trial. We're being tried together. We moved to have a sufficient amount of time to put on our case. Our case was limited in part of the time that you divvied up to everybody else. Therefore, we have no choice but -- we had no choice but to put on a limited case, and, of course, through the other accused cases, to -- either through cross-examination or, in this manner, to protect our rights. That is why. We are part and parcel of the joint criminal enterprise. And I'm not going to sit here and not make a record, particularly when it refers to a document that we tried to introduce in our case through a witness. If you may recall, Your Honour, even you, yourself, pointed out the hypocrisy of, on the one hand, the Prosecution arguing that the HVO HZ-HB was somehow siphoning up the money from the border, from the Customs, while at the same time billions of dollars is coming in through various countries, hard-line Islamic countries who are promoting an Islamic revolution, in a sense, in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. So that's why I'm intervening. I have a right to intervene. Otherwise, grant my motion to sever, and we can go on. We made that motion. But this goes to the heart, because while the Prosecution is promoting this double policy by the Croats, what we maintain -- what we maintain, that Alija Izetbegovic, as a young Muslim, way before, when the young Muslims were participating with the Nazis as part of the SS in order to create a Muslim state within Bosnia-Herzegovina, that's where it all began. And some of those, along with Alija Izetbegovic, then later on become at the very top of the SDA policy, and this policy -- and when you read the Islamic declaration which we put in for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I can't get rid of the impression that you are pleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You asked me why it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I thought that was the purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Why do you intervene? You intervene to plead?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... I have a reason to show that I have a reason for intervening and why the relevance of this document. I can't explain the relevance without giving an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But this is a witness; it's an accused in his own case. He appears as a witness, and he is questioned by able counsel. And you stand up and you comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not commenting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There was an objection. The objection was they do not wish for this document to come in. That's how it all started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, I missed the objection. I missed the objection. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was just responding to the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. I'm really sorry, because I had missed that. I do not always see the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm trying to restrain myself. I'm trying to restrain myself, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I'm also trying to make my record. Now, if the Prosecution wishes to withdraw the objection and allow the witness to comment upon it, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay, yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, the objection was relevancy, Your Honour. Now, a skillful lawyer like Mr. Karnavas can respond to an objection on relevancy grounds in three lines or less, that's number one, without making a closing statement. Now, this is the point: There was an arms embargo going on. Croatia needs to raise arms, and they're going out and trying to raise arms. Fine. Bosnia-Herzegovina is going around trying to raise arms as well. Fine. Now, but this document is being tendered as part of a submission that Croatia was aiding and helping Bosnia-Herzegovina acquire arms. The document doesn't show that. This document is irrelevant to that assertion, because this simply puts Alija Izetbegovic and others in Vienna paying money to acquire arms to -- for Bosnia-Herzegovina. It has nothing to do with any involvement or assistance from Croatia. That's the basis of the objection as being irrelevant, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to respond to my colleague, Mr. Stringer, that this document -- the point of this document is -- and the fact that Croatia, that had just been through a war and that was housing an incredible amount of refugees, is now allocating money, weapons, to aid Bosnia and Herzegovina, yet at the same time, the authorised -- the highest representatives of Bosnia and Herzegovina are gathering resources, money. And although they are in areas where they're fighting side by side with the HVO with the Croats from Bosnia and Herzegovina, these funds never reach Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say this: The stockholders of the bank are not the presidents of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, but the president of the SDA Party, Alija Izetbegovic. It's an association to aid Muslims, not citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Merhamet is an exclusively Muslim organisation. The Gazi Husrev-Begova Medresa is a Muslim religious organisation exclusively. The Preporod Cultural Society is a Muslim cultural society. The Organisation for Helping the Sahid is there to help only Muslims. Here, Alija Izetbegovic figures as a representative of the Muslim people only. He's only fighting for the Muslims. He's not a statesman; he's not representing Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this was how he conducted himself throughout this period. And I will show that quite clearly, despite the fact that at times he was treated by the West as the president of the republic. These documents and the billions that they gathered did not go into the coffers of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but only to the Muslim people. They are not buying weapons; they are taking money to fund their party, the party of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I've stated our objections. The Trial Chamber will see our objections when these documents are tendered. It seems to me now that the document is being tendered for reasons other than initially suggested, which had to do with this Croatian aid to Bosnia-Herzegovina. So there may be other reasons why it's being tendered, but that alone is relevant. Anyway, nothing more from me on this. You'll have our objections at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All this is recorded, everybody's position has been recorded. The Trial Chamber will hand down a decision when it receives submissions for documents to be tendered. Each document will be scrutinised. It takes hundreds of hours, is very time-consuming, but we'll do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, we're now moving on to humanitarian organisations on the territory of Republic of Croatia for collecting aid to the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is the next document. There are actually 276 documents and 49 sub-documents. And it starts on 3D32-1215; and in English, 3D38-0220. So can you say something about the humanitarian aid that was given to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the territory of the Republic of Croatia first?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Croatian authorities registered the right to existence with an address, names, surname of the representatives and so on, of 234 foreign humanitarian organisations. They were registered in the Republic of Croatia. And all of them tell with providing aid to Bosnia-Herzegovina and to taking care of the displaced persons and refugees. Of course, Your Honours, there were many honest people and genuine efforts to help, but of those 234 organisations, half of them were quite simply spy organisations, with all that that entails. And once the Mujahedin started arriving, and I remember when we stopped a convoy on one occasion with 21 old vans that were almost scrap and only worth a thousand Deutschemarks each, with four or five people inside them, and when we saw that it wasn't the humanitarian workers who were coming in but some people who were going to fight, then we said, Load this up on a truck; do that. But what do you need so many people for? And then, of course, they complained and said they all had IDs testifying to the fact that they belonged to humanitarian organisations and that people shouldn't be allowed to stop them. And 5.000 entered Bosnia-Herzegovina in that way. They all had IDs from some recognised humanitarian organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, the information that you referred to can be found on page 3D32-1216, and for the English, 3D38-0221. I'm going to ask you now to turn to the next page -- or, rather, we'll skip the maps and go to 3D32-1220, and in English, 3D38-0225. And with that 3D32-0221 -- or, rather, 38-2226 --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the Croatian number?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It was 32-1220, and it is an inquest register of people registered in Croatia of persons authorised to carry out humanitarian activities, and that is the list that confirms what you were saying earlier on. It was issued by the Republic of Croatia, the Ministry of Social Services, Department for Humanitarian Activities, and the date is Zagreb, May 1996. Now turn to page 3D32-1245.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just have a moment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just have a small clarification. Is it the contention of the Defence that these 234 organisations were all acting in favour -- exclusively or partly in favour of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in particular the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence isn't challenging that. The Defence is just showing which humanitarian organisations existed on the territory of Croatia and had their offices there and worked on humanitarian aid -- or, rather, aid to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. They also worked for assistance to the Republic of Croatia, partially, and to Bosnia-Herzegovina, but there are a considerable number of those who were working only for the Muslims. I know that. I have documents to bear that out. For example, when certain shipments arrived in the port of Ploce, it said, only for the Muslims, exclusively for Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the question was whether we challenged that this aid came in and that these organisations existed. That's why I said we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There's something I said got lost in translation. I did not challenge anything. Mr. Praljak has absolutely answered my question in a satisfactory way, also in a short way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't need to address those next documents which are letters of thanks, gratitude.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: We now come to the protocol on cooperation. It is 3D32-1246, and 3D38-0231 is the English version. And we've already seen this protocol in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and there's nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Fine. There is a document that I would like us to discuss now. It is 32-1247, and for the English, 3D38-0232. And it is the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons of the Government of Croatia, addressed to Professor Adalbert Rebic, the ambassador to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The date is the 19th of April, 1994. And it says, according to paragraph 1, that information is being disseminated about an increasing number of Bosnia-Herzegovinian citizens who, with the help of the UNHCR, keep arriving at the border of the Republic of Croatia, with the aim of going further on to third countries. And the ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina is sending information to Mr. Adalbert Rebic, and in that way is drawing his attention to this fact and asking for cooperation and proposals linked to that topic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know about this problem. It did exist, and later on it became even more topical. War is always a dark thing, and some organisations wanted to recruit refugees and to take them somewhere. Now, Your Honours, later on it turned out that children were being taken, and later in Bosnia and Herzegovina everyone who lives there -- well, mothers went to look for their children. They went to look for their children in Italy and other countries, children who never came back to them. In certain parts there was something that was akin to the slave trade, trading with people. But how can you intervene if this is carried out by authorised organisations? How can you stop this human trafficking? How can you find the perpetrators and arrest them? It was difficult, and I'm still reading about people searching for missing children, children who were quite simply seized and never returned, and they were taken over, allegedly, for humanitarian reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 3D32-1253 is the document I'd like us to look at next, and it is 3D38-0238 for the English. The date is the 16th of September, 1993, and the proclamation was written in Zagreb on behalf of the Mesihat, signed by Mr. Omer Pasic. Do you know this man, Mr. Omer Pasic, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we know each other and have for quite some time. Mr. Sefko Omerbasic is the number-one man in the Islamic community in Croatia. And then we have Dr. Izet Aganovic. He was at the university, and he worked in the Croatian government, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And what about Caritas for the Republic of Croatia, Andjelika Okic or Cokic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know who that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Anyway, it is a humanitarian organisation with its seat in Zagreb, and humanitarian organisations in Zagreb are launching an appeal and saying that they're concerned about the situation that both the Orthodox Muslims and Catholics are finding themselves in. I think that we can skip over the next documents, which are in Arabic, although we do have the English translations of them, but I don't have the English to hand so I can't deal with those just now.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have a letter to the Main Staff of the HVO, dated the 9th of June, 1993. The deputy commander, Stjepan Siber speaks about a helicopter -- helicopters going from Split to Tuzla and back, transporting the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That is 3D32-1255, and the English is -- well, I don't seem to have the English, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, never mind. On the 9th of June, 1993, it says: "To the Main Staff of the HVO and deputy commander of the BH Army." Stjepan Siber sent a letter about the intended helicopter fly-overs, BH helicopter fly-overs. And it says that they will be making transports from Tuzla to Split, that they will be transporting the wounded. And as far as I know, this was all respected and adhered to, but General Petkovic will be able to tell you more about that when his turn comes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Okay, let's move on. We have a document about the purchase of satellite telephone devices, which was recorded on 3D32-1260; English, 3D38-0241. The date is Vienna, 19 March 1993. Twenty satellite telephone devices for Bosnia. Hasan Cengic, who took them over.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Do you know if the HVO received any of the satellite telephones?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a single one. I know how many -- how much telecommunication things we released through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the HVO. I and Minister Susak approved the contingent for a gentleman whose name we won't mention because he is protected. However, we never received anything from the BiH Army. I'm not talking only about telephones; nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I believe we can go on to a new file called "The Assistance to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina via Croatian Harbours." The first page is 3D32-1265, and the first English page is 3D38-0246. The total number of documents is 223, and our file contains 40 of them. General, you've already mentioned harbours. You mentioned -- first of all, can you tell us how we collected documents relative to the harbours?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A person from the Defence team went to Ploce Harbour and spent two months there digging in the cellar to ferret out the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. We have some witness statements. They worked between 1992 and 1995 in the harbours, and they can confirm the veracity and authenticity of all the documents. If we go to page 3D32-1269, English 3D38-0248, we are in the year 1993. I skipped a few. This is a list of arrivals in Ploce Harbour of various ships. This lists the names of the ships, the type of cargo, the shipper, and the addressee or the recipient of the cargo. We're starting with the 19th of February, 1993, and we cover the entire year 1993. We can see that humanitarian aid arrived in Ploce. The Red Cross of the Republic of Croatia sends things for the Green Crescent of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Again, in June the Red Cross sends flour for the Green Crescent of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May 1993, you can see -- well, never mind that. It doesn't -- it's diesel fuel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Diesel fuel?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Diesel fuel. You know diesel fuel went to the BH Army in continuity. There was never any quibble about that, although that was useful, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, for the helicopters, for the tanks, for all the vehicles that they had. The entire Bosnian Army used it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It strikes me that under the 2nd July 1993, I note a shipment of wine. Were the Muslims given wine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, just --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D32 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: On second look, I see, on the right-hand column: "Import to RH." So this is not all stuff that came in from the Muslims -- for the Muslims, but it's mixed; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour, not only for the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, this is not only for the Muslims. However, save for the cargo that was let through, this is actually export, and 90 percent of -- or maybe even more than that is export for Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's the destination of the cargo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: In the last column, you can see the recipient, addressee who's going to receive the cargo that arrived in the harbours. And it says "BiH." It's in the list. So as you go through the months of that year in the last right-hand side column, you can see exactly who the cargo was intended for. For example, 10 July 1993, the UNHCR, Metkovic sends something from BiH, but also there was flour from Caritas in Medjugorje. This is just an overview of what was happening. The general has already told us that Ploce Harbour was used to handle any kind of assistance.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ploce Harbour is in Croatia, and the assistance went to Bosnia-Herzegovina, lots of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: On page 3D32-1274; English 3D38-0256, through 3D32-1276 and 3D38-0258, or maybe 7, is the transcript of the audio-recording of the 172nd Session of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in from October 1992. On page 2, which is 3D32-1275, i.e., 3D38-0257, a person by the name Zlatko interrupted the session. Actually, he bursts in the session and informs everybody that 20.000 tonnes of oil had arrived in Split from Turkey. You said it yourself, General, the diesel fuel and oil kept on arriving throughout all that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And this document shows that the oil arrived either for the Merhamet or the citizens of Sarajevo. However, it arrived in Split?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only for Merhamet.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: There is a discussion about that, and you say it's for the Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I say.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Do you wish to look at another document in the file about the humanitarian aid and the assistance of harbour? There is the import of fuel into BiH through Croatian harbours. It starts at 3D32-1289, in English it is 3D38-0261. D38-0261. This is where the documents start. Do you want to go through each of them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. These are documents at everybody's disposal, and at the end we can see the tonnes total. We're talking about hundreds of thousands of tonnes, maybe several hundred thousands of tonnes through the harbour of Ploce. We did not have the capabilities to investigate all the harbours. Croatia has not done that. It's only normal. So we are talking about harbours Ploce, Split, Pula, Istra, Rasa, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can we now skip these documents and move on to the next file, which is treating the wounded soldiers of the BiH Army and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise to counsel for the interruption. Mr. President, just as we reach the last final minutes of this week's trial proceedings, I'd like to ask the Trial Chamber for just two minutes to address something before we adjourn today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
